newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Ukraine stock market wants to grow up.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ukraine stock market wants to grow up.

text.p: Ukraine's stock market is casting off its child's play reputation and turning into what dealers and investors say is the next place to be in emerging markets.

"Everybody is here, everybody is waiting," said Alexander Parshakov, managing partner of Finance and Credit Invest, one of the first stockbrokers in the country of 51 million people which won independence from the Soviet Union six years ago.
A flurry of foreign and local investment companies has been busy opening doors in the capital, keeping an eye on impending privatisations to activate the sleepy market.
"The most important thing that will happen is that energy companies will privatise," Parshakov said.
"Investors are looking for attractive shares in the market, but now the market is small and trade volumes are very low."

The market in the former Soviet republic, which has earned an unhappy billing for slow economic reforms, sluggish privatisation and pitiful foreign investment, has at best been described as embryonic and at worst as serious as a bingo game.

Often only the hardiest investors, some of them turned away from the Treasury bill market because of falling yields, have forged into a stock market which has neither a depositary, registration system, nor clearing centres.
But all that could be about to change with the launch of a new index and government promises to speed up privatisation.
STOCK MARKET GROWING SLOWLY

Activity has increased slowly on the year-old, Kiev-based PFTS OTC Stock Trading System, listing about 130 companies and estimated to account for 80 percent of primary market and up to 20 percent of secondary market activity.

OTC officials expect to beat their record weekly turnover to date of $4.5 million soon, especially if government plans to privatise some 1,500 large and medium enterprises this year, including 31 electrical energy companies, succeed.

"If the government privatises all the energy enterprises it has promised to privatise, it won't be as large a market as in Russia. But now where there are one million hryvnias per day, in the future there will be one million dollars per day," Juliya Klymenko, the OTC's enforcement director, said.
Tiny volumes are also traded at the Kyiv International Stock Exchange with turnover of about $45,000 in 1996, and the Donetsk Stock Exchange, whose turnover totalled some $80,000 last year.
The Ukrainian Interbank Currency Exchange is poised to become the newest player -- it has announced plans to start trading shares on July 16.
The wallflower at the dance, the Ukrainian Stock Exchange (USE) and its 29 affiliates, is used mainly by the State Property Fund to list shares in firms no one else wants.
Modern computers, a gift from the French government, sit unused during weekly sessions when often not a single share is traded and where weekly trading averages just $200,000.

"The Ukrainian stock market was created for privatisation through certificates, and the current structure reflects this process," Oleg Mozgovoy, head of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) told a recent stock markets conference.
INVESTORS NEED A SUCCESS STORY

The need for a functioning equities market has not been lost on economic officials like central bank governor Viktor Yushchenko, who told businessmen this would be the year the stock market takes off because of privatisations.
"If the corporate market doesn't work, the central bank will very soon have trouble keeping the hryvnia stable," he said.

But dealers said there were too few personnel to run a registry, the hardworking SEC had too little clout, and Soviet-educated executives did not understand the benefits of raising money through shares -- resulting in thin trade, low liquidity and high valuations.
"They need a success story," Parshakov said.
"There are no clearing centres or depositaries, which makes buying and selling very complicated," said Bohdan Kotchoubey, an analyst with London-based Pictet.

Although some investors doubted Ukraine's State Property Fund would veer from the plodding course it has followed, others pointed to macro-economic improvements such as slowed inflation and a new currency for boosting confidence.

"Five years ago Ukraine had other issues. Others (Soviet-bloc countries) didn't have to learn how to be a country," said Joseph Kolb, general director of the U.S.-based Ladenburg Thalmann Ukrainian Securities.

Ukraine's need to nation-build when the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991 and heal a rift between Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking parts of the country was partly to blame for the fact that its stock market was three years behind Russia's and four years behind Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic.
NEW INDEX COULD PULL IN FOREIGN BUYERS
Kolb's outfit plans in September to issue Ukrainian Depositary Certificates and launch an index of 50 top stocks in the hope of pulling in foreign investors.
"My view is the gap can be closed very rapidly in Ukraine and it won't take three to four years to close it," he said.
The index would compete with the Prague-based Wood and Company's index of the OTC's top 15 firms, launched only this month and called Wood15.

The SEC's Mozgovoy also said Ukraine could launch a national index in the early part of 1998, but said the stock market was not developed enough at the moment to properly determine market capitalisation.
Kolb's plans may help calm investors nervous about Ukraine's record-six month delay on the 1997 budget, a key step for a multi-billion dollar International Monetary Fund credit.
Johann Jonach, president of Alfa Capital, said his company expected continued success but added things must change. "For serious big foreign investors it's off limits," he said.
He drew a comparison to the Russian market, where he said trading began before an infrastructure was even in place.
"In Ukraine everything is developed but there is not so much to trade."

Kolb said Ukraine needed to issue a "command decision" forcing businesses to switch to international accounting systems as most run two sets of books to avoid punitive taxes -- a problem which could be eased by tax reforms due to be considered by parliament this year.
"International players can't keep the fire going, but they can start it," Kolb said.
